t: #3603 Minimum Cost Path with Alternating Directions II — Grid DP
o: Movement is rigid: enter a cell (paying (i+1)(j+1)), then if you continue you must wait one second there (paying waitCost), then move right/down. So a path's cost = entry costs of all visited cells + wait costs of all visited cells except the start (you leave the start on second 1 immediately) and except the destination (you stop there). This gives a simple DAG DP over right/down moves: F[i][j] = entry(i,j) + min(F[i−1][j] + wait(i−1,j), F[i][j−1] + wait(i,j−1)), with F[0][0] = 1 and the start contributing no wait. Rolling arrays handle m·n up to 10^5. Verified against all three examples (9, 3, 16).
k: Waits attach to cells you depart from — never at the start, never at the destination.
Only right/down moves exist, so the grid is a DAG and one forward DP pass suffices.
Define A[i][j] = F[i][j] + wait(i,j) for departable cells (A[0][0] = 1) to make transitions uniform.

a.n: Approach 1: Row-by-row DP with rolling arrays
a.i: Keep A, the 'depart cost' of the previous row, and build the current row left to right: F = entry + min(A_from_above, A_from_left), then A = F + wait. The answer is the final F at (m−1, n−1), which correctly excludes the destination's wait.
s: Initialize A[0][0] = 1 and fill row 0: F = (j+1) + A[j−1], A[j] = F + wait[0][j].
For each later row: F[i][0] = (i+1) + A_prev[0]; A[i][0] = F + wait[i][0].
Fill the rest: F = (i+1)(j+1) + min(A_prev[j], A_cur[j−1]); A = F + wait.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, m, n, waitCost):
        INF = float('inf')
        A = [INF] * n
        A[0] = 1
        F = 1
        for j in range(1, n):
            F = (j + 1) + A[j - 1]
            A[j] = F + waitCost[0][j]
        for i in range(1, m):
            up = A[:]
            nA = [INF] * n
            F = (i + 1) + up[0]
            nA[0] = F + waitCost[i][0]
            for j in range(1, n):
                F = (i + 1) * (j + 1) + min(up[j], nA[j - 1])
                nA[j] = F + waitCost[i][j]
            A = nA
        return F

a.t: O(m·n) — each cell processed once with O(1) transitions (m·n ≤ 10^5)
a.sp: O(n) for the two rolling rows

w: The only subtle part is the wait accounting — derive it from Example 2 (start pays no wait, destination pays no wait) before coding. Pitfalls: adding waitCost at the start or destination, and integer overflow of (i+1)(j+1) up to ~10^10 in 64-bit-unsafe languages. Follow-up: if moves could also go left/up (as in Part I), the DAG property disappears and you would need Dijkstra on an expanded (cell, parity) graph.
